matched.note: File field labelled "Upload a file" vs DR1's "Attachment". Same finding, same one-line fix. A is marginally better: it asks for the change in both language copy files, C names only copy.en.js:12 and would leave the Welsh copy behind.

Continue silently discards a part-filled document row. Same ask, and both independently identify DR1's document-type-chosen signal as the has-the-user-started test and both defer to the document-type finding for it. C is better on the frontend mechanism (the fields do post on action=continue, the handler just never reads them; names postAdd as the existing save path; notes Save and return to hub behaves the same). A is better on DR1 evidence, citing the dr1-upload-documents-continue-error screen showing the three remaining messages. Genuinely complementary rather than one dominating.

The limit is never stated before the user uploads. A folds this into one finding with the cap value; C separates it and argues the two are independently schedulable in either order — the page could state today's limit of ten without touching the cap. C also insists the bullet read from the obligation value rather than hard-code a number so the hint and the error can never disagree. The split is the better shape.

Second half of A's merged finding: cap of 10 vs DR1's 15. Same value, same file. C additionally notes the obligation file's own header comment describes the group as 0..10 and needs updating with it, and argues the band explicitly (frontend-only constant, no counterpart on the wire). A does not mention the comment.

No document-type control; the type is guessed from the filename. Both nail it and both quote DR1's thirteen options. A is materially better: it flags that DR1 spells the first option out as "Intra Trade Animal Health Certificate (ITAHC)" where the frontend's label is the bare acronym, and that the frontend's enum carries a fourteenth type (HEALTH_CERTIFICATE) DR1 does not offer — two alignment items C loses entirely. C's one addition worth keeping: a wrong guess is uncorrectable, since the only row actions are View file and Remove.

Native file button vs DR1's drop zone with a polite live region naming the chosen file. Both correctly rule that govuk-frontend's enhanced file upload already ships this rather than hand-rolling DR1's bespoke markup. C is better on the how (names govuk-frontend 6.3 and the client bundle to initialise); A is better on scope (the zone takes its own error style — the red dashed border on the error screen — and the unenhanced input stays as the no-JS fallback). Neither is complete alone.

10 MB vs DR1's 50MB. Both banded needs-backend and both found the code comment recording that 10 MB was chosen to clear the platform's nginx ingress cap — the same non-obvious reason, reached independently, which is the strongest agreement in this area. A adds MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES and the unit inconsistency ("50MB" unspaced vs "10 MB" spaced); C adds the captured client-side data-max-file-size=10000000 attribute.

Page runs as one flat column where DR1 groups the form, the add button and the saved table inside a bordered "File upload" panel with the page-level actions outside. Same fix. A is better: it names aria-labelledby and asks for the h2 to be referenced from the group so the grouping is announced as well as drawn, and points at the summary-card border as the nearest thing already in the toolbox. C says "build it from what the design system offers" without naming anything.

No guidance above the form; DR1 opens with the ITAHC paragraph, the "other documents" bullets and a details expander holding the three-row consignment table and the GOV.UK link. Near-identical, down to quoting the same three table rows. C rules the outbound-URL question itself (use the clean guidance URL, drop DR1's analytics parameters); A leaves it open but adds the better question — whether those three rows are settled content or a placeholder a content designer will replace. Take C's ruling and A's question.

JPG accepted but missing from the file-type hint. Both diagnose the same cause — the hint is collapsed on MIME type and .jpeg/.jpg share image/jpeg — and both note the truncated list is reused in the rejection message. C is marginally better evidenced, quoting the captured accept attribute in full.

Scan status labelled "Checking"/"Safe" vs DR1's "Scanning for virus"/"Check completed". Both describe DR1's visually hidden "Virus check status for {reference}" prefix, but only C carries it into the ask — A leaves it as description and never requests it, so building A's version leaves the accessibility gap in place. C also establishes that the client polling payload is generated from the same copy and so needs no separate edit, where A treats it as extra work.

Validation wording. A covers four differences, C only three — C drops the capacity message, so DR1's "You can upload a maximum of 15 files" never gets aligned against the frontend's "You can add a maximum of 10 documents". C's cap finding (inc-037) explicitly says the copy already interpolates the number and changes nothing else, so the "documents" vs "files" wording falls between C's two findings and is lost. A also lists DR1's "Select a document type" message so the document-type work inherits the right string. A is the one to build from.

onlyC.title: The documents page's primary button reads "Continue" where Design release 1 reads "Save and continue"
onlyC.why: Partial — C raises it service-wide across the documents page and the consignment addresses hub. Run A has no counterpart: A's inc-042 notes DR1 calls the button "Save and continue" but only in passing, and its ask is the discard behaviour, not the label. A's nearest button-label findings are inc-072 (identification's "Save and finish") and inc-116 ("hub" vs "overview" on the secondary actions), neither of which touches the documents page's primary button. C is right that a button which does not save should not be the only one on the page reading Continue while DR1 reserves that word for check-your-answers and the declaration. Genuinely new.

matched.note: Same finding: rows locked behind earlier answers with 'Cannot start yet'; DR1 links every row unconditionally. A is broader on the user picture (nine of eleven rows dead on a part-answered notification) and traces the prerequisite chain to obligation-source; C is better for whoever does the work — it proves no route handler consults those prerequisites (only entry-guard.js), so the pages already admit direct visits and the real cost is making each page cope with unanswered predecessors. C also gives exact DOM counts (one govuk-task-list__link, ten cannot-start-yet) as its falsifier.

Both: consignment-details has no hub row of its own, folded into 'What are you importing?'; DR1 lists 'Commodity details' first under 'Description of the goods'. Both spot the same trap — the frontend does show the words 'Commodity details' on the hub, but as a section heading, not a row. Same code citation, same fix, same caveat that the two rows' obligations must be split.

Both: 'Your commodities' totals suppressed until a commodity exists; DR1 shows the panels reading 0 from the first visit. Identical code citations and fix. C additionally carries the layout consequence that travels with it — DR1 gives the hub the full grid width while the frontend confines the panels to a two-thirds column — and says so explicitly to avoid raising it twice.

Both: the identification row is unconditional, so it shows on a notification with no commodity; DR1 inserts it only when a chosen species has identifiers. C is materially better and A is wrong on effort: A says 'the hub already has the machinery for this', C proves it does not — commodityLines is a structural group in scope from creation, so the row's status roll-up never reaches not-applicable and marking the row conditional alone leaves it drawn. C names the two ways out.

Both: no 'Review and submit' button; review is a locked task row in a sixth section. Same DR1 citation, same fix. A treats the check-answers page rendering an unfinished notification as an unmet dependency; C shows it is already met by pointing at the frontend's own captured fe-check-answers-incomplete screen, so only the route to it is missing. That materially shrinks the job.

Both: six section headings named and ordered differently, documents demoted below the addresses, contact address sharing a section instead of having its own. Same fix. A folds two extras into this one finding that C splits or handles elsewhere — the within-section row order (C's inc-043) and the 'Notification tasklist' heading (A's inc-059). C states section membership row by row, which is the more usable form for a build.

Second half of the same ground: identification should sit before additional details inside section 2. A buries this as one clause of its group-structure finding; C raises it as a finding of its own with both captures cited. C's split is the better shape — it is a one-line swap that can land independently of the renaming and regrouping.

Both: hint text on all eleven rows where DR1 has one, on 'Roles and addresses', and the frontend's hint names five parties where DR1 names four. Same wording, same fix. C is marginally better evidenced — it counts the hint elements by class on each side (eleven against one) and notes the hints roughly double the page height.

Both: the same six row labels differ, and both list the same four that already match. Both single out 'Uploaded documents' against 'Upload documents' as a change of meaning rather than a tidy-up. C gives the rename key by key (importReason, additionalDetails, animalIdentification, transporter, contact, documents), which is directly buildable.

Both: the frontend's status vocabulary is larger than DR1's two words. A is better because its capture is richer — it saw all four states rendered ('Completed', 'In progress', 'Not yet started', 'Optional' as untagged grey text) and can say what a user actually meets; C's two hub captures showed only 'Not yet started', 'Cannot start yet' and 'Completed', so C honestly declines to claim anything about 'In progress' and 'Optional' and hands the decision on where they should show back to the reader.

onlyA.title: The frontend hub carries an Exit details task DR1 does not have
onlyA.why: Not a miss — C found the same difference but gave it no hub id. C's inc-067 (import-reason) asks for the four follow-up questions to become conditional reveals under the import reason and, in its work statement, to 'delete the four pages, the conditional exit-details task row'. So the hub row's removal is inside another finding's prose. The practical difference is trackability: run A gives the hub change its own row with its own dependency on the reveals work, run C does not, so a team building C's backlog could land inc-067 and leave the hub row question unrecorded.

onlyA.title: Exit details row shown but unreachable for temporary admission of horses (rowGatePasses tests only the first page)
onlyA.why: A genuine C miss, and the strongest single item in run A's hub set. It is a live defect rather than a design difference: rowGatePasses tests row.pages[0] while rowEntry picks the first page that passes, so under temporary admission of horses — where destination country is out of scope but port of exit and exit date are mandatory — the row is dead and its real status is replaced by 'Cannot start yet'. C never captured that state (its hub shots are the empty and part-answered notification) and the string 'Exit details' appears nowhere in run C's backlog. C's inc-051 would incidentally fix it by removing row gating altogether, but C never identified the bug, so nobody reading C knows there is a defect on main today.

onlyA.title: DR1 introduces the tasks under a 'Notification tasklist' heading
onlyA.why: Half found by C, half missed. C's inc-050 names the missing 'Notification tasklist' heading in its prose and asks for it to be added, so the copy change is covered without its own id. What C misses entirely is the heading-level consequence A raises: DR1 demotes its six section captions to h3 under that h2 so the page reads as two named sections, where the frontend renders 'Your commodities' and all six captions at the same level. That is an accessibility point and it survives only in run A.

onlyC.title: Halfway through a new notification the frontend drops the user on the hub and makes them start each remaining section from it
onlyC.why: A real catch that run A missed completely, and the biggest thing run C tells a BA about this area. Run A has no finding on journey sequencing at all: it never cites src/server/app/sets/live-animals/journeys/linear/flow/run.js, never cites DR1's step list at app/routes.js:1256-1305, and no A finding in any domain describes the fall-through to the hub. C shows the frontend's opening run stops after the additional-animal-details page and every later section is a separate departure from and return to the task list, where DR1 runs origin through to declaration in one sequence and treats the hub as somewhere a user chooses to go. C is careful to separate it from row unlocking: that decides what a user can start from the list, this decides whether they are sent to the list at all. It is filed under hub but it is really a journey-flow finding, which is plausibly why A's slicing let it fall between two authors.

areas.area: Reason for import and exit details

matched.note: The headline finding on both sides: DR1 asks purpose, destination country, port of exit and exit date as conditional reveals under the chosen reason; the frontend asks each on its own page. Same diff, same reveal ordering called out (port of exit before destination country under Transit; exit date before port of exit under Temporary admission). C is materially better evidenced — it counts the extra page loads per reason, cites the four obligation gates line-by-line to prove the two sides agree on when each question applies (so no obligation moves), and its falsifier is a DOM test (no govuk-radios__conditional, no aria-controls on any radio) rather than a routing claim. A's advantage is decomposition, not evidence: it spins the hub knock-on and the hint removal out as separately shippable findings where C swallows them.

Frontend puts explanatory hint text under destination country, port of exit and exit date that DR1 does not have (and DR1 keeps only the 'For example, 27/3/2026' worked example). C found this — it is in inc-067's detail and its remedy says to drop the hints — but gave it no id of its own. A is better here purely because it is trackable: a copy-only change with its own falsifier, and A alone spots that 'Exit and entry share the same port list' becomes factually untrue the moment the exit-port list is narrowed. In C that observation survives only inside inc-069's prose.

The frontend hub carries an 'Exit details' task DR1 has no equivalent of. Again C found it but did not book it — inc-067's remedy says to delete 'the conditional exit-details task row', and inc-044 cites the same row in passing as proof the frontend knows how to hide a row. A books it as a hub finding with an explicit dependency on the reveal change. Same diff either way; A's version is the one a planner can schedule.

Both catch that the frontend promotes the question 'What is the main reason for importing the animals?' to the h1 where DR1 heads the page 'Main reason for import' and keeps the question as a visually hidden legend. C additionally catches that the frontend names the page a third thing — 'Reason for import' in the title and breadcrumb — so the page calls itself two different names in three places. A misses that entirely; it only notes the hub task row says 'Main reason for importing'.

Frontend reuses the ~78-entry port-of-entry list as the port of exit; DR1 offers ten animal-approved border control posts with BCP codes. Both banded needs-backend, both name the reference-data work and both say the 'exit and entry share the same list' hint must go. C is slightly better because it names why the frontend is wrong on purpose: the frontend's own obligation cites the V4 field spec saying exit and entry share a list, so this is a requirements conflict between V4 and the signed-off design, not a coding slip — and C flags that this ticket is where that gets settled. A presents it as a straightforward miss.

Internal-market purpose can be left blank and the user walks on; DR1 stops them with 'Select a purpose in the internal market'. C merges this with the identical exit-date gap into one finding (see next row); A keeps them apart. A's version quotes the DR1 error-summary and reveal behaviour in more detail; C's names the culprit validator (oneOf at validators.js:118 explicitly permits an empty string). Even on substance.

Second half of the same C finding: exit date can be left blank under Temporary admission horses with no message, where DR1 says 'Enter an exit date'. Both runs also spot that the frontend's 'Enter a real exit date' should be DR1's 'Enter a real date' — A tucks it into this finding's remedy, C promotes it into inc-066. C alone notices that DR1 deliberately leaves the main reason radio itself optional, so the two sides already agree there and disagree only about what hangs off it — a useful scoping fact A never states.

Identical finding, independently derived: the same four of eleven internal-market purpose hints (it's/its, the stray comma, 'e.g.' for 'for example', three missing full stops), the same two source files, the same conclusion that the other seven match word for word. The strongest agreement in the area — two agents reading the same copy file months apart produced the same four-item list.

'Select the destination country' / 'Select the port of exit' where DR1 and GDS style say 'Select a …'. C bundles in the third string, 'Enter a real exit date' → 'Enter a real date', so the whole exit-message copy change is one ticket; A splits that third string off into inc-083. C also remembers the Welsh copy files, which A does not mention anywhere in this area.

onlyA.title: A user importing horses temporarily cannot get back to their port of exit and exit date from the hub — the Exit details row is shown but has no link
onlyA.why: A genuine miss by C, and the most valuable single item in this area because it is a live defect rather than a parity gap. Under Temporary admission horses the Exit details row stands for three pages, of which the first (destination country) is out of scope; rowGatePasses tests only row.pages[0] (flow/navigation.js:25) where rowEntry two lines above already picks the first page that passes, so the row renders as dead text tagged 'Cannot start yet' and the user can never return to answer they have already given. C's inc-051 proposes deleting hub row gating wholesale, which would fix this incidentally, but C never observes the temporary-admission dead end, never identifies the pages[0] bug, and never notes that blockedRowItem overwrites the row's real status. Grepping C for 'rowGatePasses' returns inc-051 only, and inc-051 is about a fresh notification with ten locked rows, not this case. A also proposes it as a one-line fix worth shipping ahead of the larger reveal change — C has no equivalent cheap remedy anywhere.

onlyC.title: Check your answers never shows the exit answers — destination country, exit date and port of exit — so a trader cannot see or change them from the review page
onlyC.why: A genuine miss by run A. A has fifteen review findings and none of them notices the omission; grepping A's backlog for 'destination country', 'port of exit' or 'exit date' returns only origin- and hub-domain findings, nothing in review. C proves it from source both ways: the reason-for-import card builds exactly four possible rows (additional-animal-details.js:18-54) and the check-answers copy file has no key for any of the three, while DR1 adds a row per exit answer to its Main reason for import card (routes.js:4640-4669). C is honest that its confidence is medium — both runs captured the review page with the reason set to Re-entry, which puts all three questions out of scope, so neither side's screenshot shows the rows and both halves are read from code. That is almost certainly why A missed it: A worked from the same picture and the picture shows nothing. One caveat for the BA — C's aside that DR1 also has a separate 'Exit border control post' row looks like a misreading of DR1's own field name transitExitBorderControlPost, which is the transit reveal's port-of-exit field, not a sixth question; C excludes it from the finding anyway.

matched.note: Page name 'Consignment details' vs DR1's 'Commodity details'. Same finding, same one copy string carrying h1/tab/breadcrumb, same fix. Both correctly park the section caption ('About the consignment') as a separate service-wide difference. Nothing to choose between them.

'Help with commodity codes' — one sentence vs DR1's three paragraphs plus the Trade Tariff link. Word-for-word the same finding, same fix (the copy entry has to become HTML). C edges it only on evidence: its falsifier is discharged against the captured DOM ('the only link in main content is Cancel and return to hub'), where A asserts it.

The inset on 'What are you importing?' drops DR1's second sentence — a consignment needing no health certificate must still be notified. Identical finding, identical citation, and both independently say take DR1's whole two-sentence wording rather than appending, because the first sentence is inverted too.

Checkbox list of the whole catalogue vs DR1's search control. Same finding, and both describe the results panel and the selected-items panel with its count and Clear all. They split the extra detail: A has the persistence mechanism (selections seeded back as JSON) and ties the work to sourcing the real catalogue first; C has the three-character threshold, the bold match highlighting, and the instruction to keep the existing 'Select a commodity' error. A BA gets more from reading both than from either.

Number of animals accepts a blank. Both trace it to the same allow('') in integerInRange and both cite the frontend's own test asserting the blank saves. C is tighter on the fix (it names the exact message to add, 'Enter the number of animals') and on the consequence chain — the user is not lost, only stopped later at the gated review with no reason given. A is tighter on the knock-on: once blank cannot be saved, the count-drop check has no live case, and the test has to change.

Packages labelled '(optional)' where DR1 says '(when required)'. Same finding, same one-line fix. C is the more useful write-up because it flags the open question: neither side validates the box for live animals today, so if 'when required' turns out to mean a rule rather than a hint, that rule is separate work and DR1 never states it. A asserts the two sides already agree it is not enforced and stops there.

Species offered as bare Latin binomials where DR1 shows 'Common name (Latin name)'. Both get the rule and the fallback right. A is materially better evidenced — 123 of DR1's 144 species carry a common name, the fallback is 'Sheep (Ovis aries)', and the common name is what DR1's search matches and orders on, so this has to land before the search control ships. C's one advantage is band honesty: it flags that the band moves to needs-backend if the live commodity service turns out not to carry a common name per species.

onlyA.title: A user can declare only five commodities and eight species in the frontend, where DR1 offers 21 live-animal commodities under their IPAFFS names and 144 species between them.
onlyA.why: Not a C miss — a scope rule. C's finding contract excludes 'what a stub happens to contain' (FINDING-CONTRACT.md:415-436: both catalogues are fixture data, and if swapping the fixture for real data makes the difference go away it is not a finding). C knows the numbers — its inc-022 cites the twenty-one commodities and the hundred-plus species under Other live mammals — it just refuses to raise the catalogue itself. Worth knowing this is the only needs-backend item in A's commodities area and the largest piece of work in it. The structural half A folded into this finding, the per-species rows for 01061900, C raised on its own as inc-016 and showed it needs no backend at all.

onlyA.title: The frontend puts an example hint under Number of animals — 'For example, 1, 25 or 5000.' — that DR1 does not have.
onlyA.why: A genuine C miss. C read the same template block closely enough to write a typography finding about its labels and hints (inc-017) and quoted the packages hint verbatim in inc-024, but never noticed the animals hint has no DR1 counterpart. Not an application change either: the string is still at copy.en.js:29 in the frontend today.

onlyC.title: For commodity code 01061900 Design release 1 lists each chosen species as its own removable row in Selected commodities; Frontend gives the commodity one row and one Remove that drops every species under it.
onlyC.why: Inside A inc-017's prose, with no id of its own — A lists 'the selected-commodities table gains the per-species row and per-species Remove' as one of three things that follow once the real catalogue arrives. C is materially better here and the difference matters commercially: A has this blocked behind a reference-data API, C shows it is a table-and-Remove change against today's stub, because the store already holds one line per species and only the page collapses them. C also shows the difference is visible today with one species each — DR1's row reads 'Domestic dog', the frontend's reads 'Dog'.

onlyC.title: On the commodity-details page Frontend sets the commodity heading, the species name and the quantity labels smaller and lighter than Design release 1, so the page loses the reading order the design gives it.
onlyC.why: A genuine A miss. Typography was in scope for A — it raised exactly this kind of finding for the origin page (its inc-129) — and A has no service-wide type finding that would swallow this one. C measures it: 36px bold commodity heading, 24px species name, 19px bold labels against 19px light hints, cited to the app-consignment-details-page block in the prototype stylesheet.

onlyC.title: Frontend refuses to let a user lower the number of animals below the identification records already entered for that species; Design release 1 accepts the lower number and shows only that many records.
onlyC.why: A genuine A miss, and the sharpest one in the area — it is a behaviour difference that stops a user dead, with an error whose summary link sends them to the identification card rather than the box they typed in. A knew the rule was there: it names the count-drop check twice inside inc-023 as a knock-on of making the count mandatory, but never compares it to DR1, which runs four validators on that page and none of them reads the saved identifiers. C also flags the open decision the fix carries: what happens to the surplus record.

onlyC.title: Removing the last commodity leaves the Frontend user on an empty details page with a link to start again; Design release 1 takes them straight back to "What are you importing?".
onlyC.why: A genuine A miss. A's backlog has no mention of the empty state, the 'You have not added any commodities yet.' copy or the post-remove handler anywhere. Neither side photographed the state, so both halves are read from source — C says so, and names the observation that would settle it.

onlyC.title: When a count is not a whole number Frontend says "Number of animals must be a whole number, like 25"; Design release 1 says "Enter a whole number greater than 0".
onlyC.why: A genuine A miss, and a near one: A quotes DR1's exact string 'Enter a whole number greater than 0' inside inc-023 as what DR1 shows for a non-numeric value, but never checks it against the frontend's own message and never quotes the frontend's. C adds that the one frontend string covers both failure modes, so a user who types 0 is told to enter a whole number, which 0 already is.

matched.note: Arrival date hint states the valid window; DR1 gives a worked example. Same ask, same evidence lines, near-identical prose. A adds one thing C does not — a decision to take on whether the example date stays hard-coded (it goes stale within the year); C adds one A does not — that the picker's bounds and the out-of-range error already enforce the window, so nothing is lost by dropping the sentence.

Means of transport as four radios vs DR1's "Select one" dropdown. Identical ask. C is materially better because it says out loud that this one runs AGAINST GOV.UK Design System advice (radios are correct for four options) and tells the reviewer to expect it to look backwards — exactly the warning a BA needs before ruling. A instead editorialises in the title ("reads as a bigger question than the page treats it as"), which is an opinion dressed as an observation. Note also: the dr1a-digest.txt band column says "disputed" for this row where the backlog says frontend-work — A's digest bands are unreliable across this whole slice, use the backlog.

No route to record a commercial transporter that is not one of the two shipped records. Both enumerate DR1's add-commercial field set identically. C is better on two counts: it names the workaround a trader actually has today (go back and declare the same firm as private, which lands a wrong type and no approval number on the notification), and it resolves the Northern Ireland restriction inside the finding — Country locked to NI, hint stated on the chooser — rather than parking it. A instead splits NI out into a disputed sibling (inc-123) and leaves this finding blocked on two unsettled decisions.

Transporter phone field has no country-code hint. C is the better-shaped increment: it carries the label change ("Telephone number" → "Phone number") and the two validation messages that quote the field name into the same edit. A splits the label into a service-wide finding (inc-001) and leaves inc-127 as hint-only, so a builder taking A's ticket ships a hint under a label DR1 does not use.

Private transporter postcode labelled "Postal or zip code" vs DR1's "Postcode or Zip code". Cross-domain pairing — A raises it once, service-wide, covering both this form and the permanent-address block; C raises it per form and says explicitly why (the strings live in separate per-feature copy files, so they are two edits not one). A's framing is the better story for a content decision; C's is the better unit of work. Both are right about the same defect.

Transit countries as 31 checkboxes vs DR1's type-ahead plus a removable list. Same ask, near-identical prose. A is marginally better evidenced on the twelve-country cap: it cites DR1's JavaScript (search box and button disabled at twelve, screen-reader message "Maximum of 12 countries reached...") with the file and line numbers, so the cap's new behaviour is specified rather than described. C gets the live-region requirement but not the disabling.

Frontend blocks an empty transit-country list; DR1 treats it as optional. Both cite the same DR1 route lines and the same obligation file. C is better because it names the precise edit (keep inScope: true and its reason, drop status: 'mandatory') and is honest that DR1's negative could only be proven from the handler, not from a capture — it says so in the FALSIFIED BY. A asserts the same conclusion without flagging that the evidence is code-only.

Transport identification hint runs four alternatives together with semicolons; DR1 bullets them. Effectively the same finding word for word, same file and line, same remediation (the copy string has to become a lead-in plus items so the template can render a list). Nothing separates them.

Page headed "Search for an approved commercial transporter" with nothing to search. A is better on mechanism: it records that DR1's filter is JavaScript-only — the search button is type="button" and the form post reads the search field then ignores it — so a no-JS user gets no filtering, which is a real requirement decision for a GOV.UK service. C says the box "filters the list as the user types", which glosses over both the button and the progressive-enhancement gap.

A raises only the missing Approved/New status tag. C raises the whole list rendering — radio-with-run-on-hint vs DR1's table with Name, Address, Approval number, Type and Status columns plus a View details link — so C's is the finding that actually changes the page, and it correctly defers the View details link to the address-book question. A keeps one point C misses and it is a good one: marking the two existing records "Approved" asserts something nothing verified, so someone has to own the list before the column can be filled.

The parent finding on both sides: DR1 opens the task on one searchable list and asks commercial-or-private only when adding; the frontend asks the type first and forks the journey. Both name it as the parent the other transporter findings hang off. C is slightly better evidenced — it lists DR1's eight records with their types (four Commercial, four Private) to prove the list is genuinely mixed, and draws the consequence A does not: a trader whose private transporter is already known has no list to pick it from and retypes the address. A's version is stronger on the ordering of the rewrite itself.

onlyA.title: A private transporter typed into one notification is not kept for reuse; in DR1 it joins the transporter list and can be picked next time
onlyA.why: Genuine C miss, and the only needs-backend item in the area. I searched run C's whole backlog for privateTransporter, "transporter" and the reuse language: C's inc-113 and inc-124 both DESCRIBE DR1's added transporter joining the list, and C's address-book finding (inc-003) records that DR1's book carries a Transporter address type — so C had every fact in hand and never turned it into an ask. Nothing in C asks for a transporter to live anywhere other than the notification. This is the one finding in the slice that needs persistence work outside the frontend, so its absence from C is the most consequential single gap.

onlyC.title: The frontend dashboard always has an ordering applied and has no unsorted state; DR1's sort control loads on "Select one"

So this is the classic hiding-inside-another-finding case — but the two runs reach opposite conclusions, and C is the more defensible. C treats the design's own page list as the specification rather than looking for a rule behind it, and its list is derived from screens not memory: origin, cph-number, contact-address, transporter-add and transporter-add-private, which overlaps A's list on three and differs on two. C also spots what A does not — DR1's private-transporter page carries a cancel link to a THIRD destination, the dashboard, not the overview — and identifies the shared macro at save-actions.njk:3-13 as taking no argument that could drop a control, so the fix is one flag rather than five shortened button groups. A BA should treat this as C's most substantive new item after inc-104.

areas.area: Addresses, contact and the address book

matched.note: Party named "Consignor or exporter" vs DR1's "Consignor". Same diff, same one copy string. C is marginally better: it proves the string is authored in exactly one place by grep, and shows the frontend already says "Consignor" on check-answers, the dashboard and its own error message — so the service contradicts itself today. A only spotted the error-message contradiction.

Contact page explains the control, not the role. Both quote DR1's sentence verbatim and both say move it from fieldset hint to body copy. C adds the useful observation that DR1 reuses that same sentence as the Branch Address type hint, and explains what the frontend's sentence actually records (contact is stored as a copy, the other four parties as references) — so a person can see nothing is lost by dropping it.

Contact list should be the trader's GB branch addresses only, not the whole book. C folded this into its role-typing finding as one clause. A gives it its own id, and A is right to: DR1 draws the contact list from a separate data file (contact-addresses.js), not from a filtered consignment book, and A's evidence names the four overseas records a trader can wrongly pick as the person responsible inside GB. Inside C inc-014 that risk is one sentence and easy to lose.

Pickers offer the whole undifferentiated book instead of the addresses saved for that role. Both band it needs-backend, both cite the same "addresses have no type" service contract. C's evidence is stronger: it shows the place-of-origin and consignee pickers are byte-identical in captured DOM, and gives DR1's per-role counts (9/9/6/6/3) and its seven-type list. A's example — a Danish meat exporter selectable as origin, consignee and importer — is the more vivid one-liner.

CPH page heading is a title-cased noun phrase where DR1 gives an instruction. Same diff. C is better scoped: it counts three spellings of the term across two pages, names all three copy files including check-answers, and carries DR1's lower-casing through the hub row and hint. A covers only the h1 and the hub row.

"What is a CPH number?" expander missing entirely. Near-identical findings, same DR1 source lines, both flag the placeholder GOV.UK href. A is marginally better because it quotes both paragraphs verbatim, so the copy can be lifted straight out; C paraphrases them.

CPH taken as one free-text box where DR1 uses three boxes sized 2/3/4. Same diff, same widths and maxlengths. A is better on the trap: it records that DR1 itself validates nothing on this page, so the frontend's nine-digit check is the stricter behaviour and must be kept rather than copied away. C notes, usefully, that DR1's three labels are screen-reader-only.

Addresses hub shows the chosen party's name and no address. Same diff, same evidence line in the controller. C is better framed: it says explicitly that the requirement is that the address is visible, not that the component matches DR1's headed-section-plus-inset, and points out the address does reappear on check-answers. A prescribes replacing the summary list outright, which is a bigger change than the finding needs.

No way to add a new address from any picker or the contact page. C is materially better evidenced: it captured the no-matches state, so it can show a page that literally cannot be satisfied, and it names DR1's add-from-picker screen and the return-preselected-plus-banner behaviour. C also bands it frontend-work on the ground that the address-book API already serves create, where A bands it needs-backend — C's band is the defensible one, since the read-only client is a design decision, not a missing backend. A carries something C does not: the workspace has already accepted this gap as a deliberate temporary measure, so it must not be treated as the next thing to fix.

"View details" expands in place where DR1 links out to the saved record. Same diff. C goes further and is better: it names the return parameter, captured DR1's record and edit pages, and shows the row leads to edit and delete — so the user need is correcting a wrong saved address, not just reading it. Again C bands frontend-work (the API serves update and delete) where A bands needs-backend. A's extra is worth keeping: the disclosure duplicates three lines already in the row, which should be dropped when the link lands.

Picker pages five at a time behind a submit-to-search where DR1 lists everything and filters live. Both are strong, both flag the no-JS constraint DR1 does not have. A is marginally better on consequences: it spots that the "Selected address:" inset exists only to work around pagination and can be deleted once the chosen row is always on screen. C has the better picture — a captured filtered state showing "Romania" narrowing 9 to 3 without a reload.

No "Same as consignee" / "Same as place of origin" copy shortcut on the hub. Same three rows, same availability rules, both note the frontend states the shortcut in the importer hint and then withholds it. C is better on the implementation trap: place of origin is stored inline while the other four are stored as references, so copying origin onto consignor must copy the record, not the reference. A asserts the opposite — that a party answer is now a reference so no data is duplicated — which is wrong for that one row.

Permanent address buried in the animal identification card instead of being its own step in the addresses section. A raises the whole permanent-address story as one finding; C splits it into three (this one, the same-as-destination reuse, and the guidance). C's split is the more buildable, and it names the ordering dependency. A caught one thing C did not: DR1 asks this for the whole 01061900 group — cat, dog, ferret and other live mammals — where the frontend asks only for cats and dogs.

Second of C's three splits of A inc-012: no "Same as the place of destination (POD)" option, so the trader retypes the address once per animal. Identical in substance, both quote the 48-hour hint, both note the destination is already on the notification. No material difference in quality.

Third of C's splits: the page guidance. A asks for DR1's two-bullet APHA definition and the 48-hour sentence. C asks for those plus two things A never mentions — the govukWarningText "Providing a false address is an act of fraud" and the question heading "Where will their permanent address be?". The fraud warning is a genuine C-only catch inside an otherwise matched pair.

"Postal or zip code" / "Telephone number" vs DR1's "Postcode or Zip code" / "Phone number" on the permanent-address block. A raises it once, service-wide, covering the transporter form and the permanent-address block together — the better structural call. But A misses the third half of the diff on this form: DR1 hints the phone field "For international numbers include the country code" and the frontend does not. A raises that hint only for the transporter form (its inc-127), never for the permanent address. C splits the finding per form and catches the hint here.

onlyA.title: DR1 asks for a CPH number on every consignment except horses and the 01061900 group; the frontend asks only when the consignment contains cattle.
onlyA.why: A genuine miss by C. C has no finding anywhere about when the CPH question applies — grep for the frontend's CPH_COMMODITIES allow-list, or for horses, returns nothing in C's backlog. This is the one address-area finding that is invisible on a captured screen: you only see it by reading the commodity rules on both sides, and A's point is the structural one — the frontend's rule is an allow-list of one ('Cow') so every commodity added in future is silently exempt, where DR1 makes CPH the default and exempts two codes. C's evidence does not contradict it; C simply never looked at applicability here.

onlyA.title: The frontend's CPH example teaches a 3/3/3 grouping that no CPH number uses; DR1's example is 12/345/6789.
onlyA.why: Inside a C finding without its own id. C inc-006 quotes both hint strings and folds the wording change into the three-box rebuild. A is right to separate it: the current example is factually wrong today, it is a one-string fix, and it does not need the three-box work to land. A person reading C's backlog would only fix it as a side effect of a larger change they might defer.

onlyA.title: The review page labels the contact address row 'Address'; DR1 labels it 'Contact address'.
onlyA.why: C missed it. C authored sixteen review-page findings and none of them touches the contact-address row label; grep for "Contact address for this consignment" in C returns only hub task-name and incomplete-summary findings. Small, but real, and it sits in the review domain rather than addresses in both runs — flagging it here because it is a contact-address diff, and the review-area comparison may count it too.

onlyC.title: Design release 1 gives a trader a saved address book they can search, filter by type, add to, view, edit and delete; Frontend has no address-book page and its journey can only read the book
onlyC.why: Structural, not a miss: run A's corpus deliberately excluded every address-book screen, so A had no pictures to author from. A's only trace of it is a clause inside its navigation finding (inc-118), which says the Address book nav item 'cannot be wired until an address-book page exists'. C photographed all eight DR1 address-book screens and enumerated them, and then stated the scope question rather than deciding it — which is why a person later marked it disputed and dropped. Two things in it are new information regardless of that ruling: trade-imports-ins-frontend already implements this book at DR1's own URLs with DR1's nine field labels, and DR1's seven address types are unbuilt everywhere, including in the address-book API's locked wire contract. That second point is what makes C inc-014 / A inc-013 a real backend gap rather than a filter someone forgot.

onlyC.title: Frontend's Consignment addresses page offers every unanswered party a link reading just "Add"; Design release 1 names the party in the link — "Add a place of origin", "Add a consignor"
onlyC.why: Hiding inside A inc-002's prose. A quotes DR1's add link 'Add a consignor' while making its Consignor-naming argument, and never notices that the frontend renders six identical anchors reading 'Add' with the party in visually hidden text. A's hub finding (inc-010) rewrites the answered rows only. So A had the evidence in hand and did not raise the diff. C is right that it is a separate, smaller change from the answered-row rewrite, and says so explicitly.

onlyC.title: Frontend squeezes the address picker's five-column results table into the narrow form column, so every row wraps onto three lines; Design release 1 gives the picker the full page width
onlyC.why: A missed it outright — no finding in A's 133 mentions column width, grid-column-full or the two-thirds surface. C's reasoning is careful in a way that matters: DR1 widens this page and not its two sibling addresses pages, so it is a per-page decision, not a house style, and the frontend already has the full-width surface and uses it on the dashboard — one line in the picker controller. C also correctly sequences it after the pagination change. This is the clearest single thing run C tells a reader that run A does not.

onlyC.title: Frontend gives the list of addresses no heading and captions it "Showing 5 of 13 addresses"; Design release 1 heads it "Select an address" and counts "Showing 9 out of 9 results"
onlyC.why: Partly inside A inc-014's prose. A quotes both DR1 strings — the 'Select an address' heading and the 'Showing 9 out of 9 results' count — and its action asks only to 'put the count line above the table'. It never asks for the heading and never asks for the count to be reworded. And A never looks at the contact-address page, which has neither a heading nor a count at all. C covers both surfaces and gives the exact replacement wording.

onlyC.title: Frontend asks which country the animals will permanently live in; Design release 1 does not ask for a country on the permanent address
onlyC.why: A genuine miss by C's favour. A inc-001 reads the same permanent-address block closely enough to cite its postcode and phone labels by line number, but never counts the fields: the frontend asks for a mandatory Country select over thirty-two options where DR1 asks for eight fields and no country. It is also the one finding in this whole area where the frontend asks for MORE than the signed-off design — a direction A's corpus looked for rarely — and C argues it well: an address APHA can inspect is a GB address, so there is nothing to choose.

matched.note: Both: country of origin is a scroll-only select in the frontend, a type-to-filter search box in DR1. A goes further — it describes the hidden value field, the aria-live match-count announcement, and flags that DR1's control degrades to a bare text input so the real service needs a no-JS fallback (select or server-rendered results page). C says nothing about JavaScript degradation, which is the one thing on this finding that could sink the ticket.

Both: the origin page's three question labels are a size down from DR1, and the internal-reference one is plain body text. C's verification is the stronger evidence — it measured DR1's app-eu-heading-m at 24px/700 against the frontend's 19px bold and 19px regular from the SCSS, and it corrects a factual slip A makes: DR1 marks the country question up as an <h2>, not a label, so a developer following A's wording will look for a heading element that has no counterpart. C also records that DR1 bolds the revealed region-code label too, and deliberately parks it inside its region-code finding rather than double-counting.

Both: DR1 shows a country-derived read-only prefix and asks only for the suffix; the frontend asks for the whole code in a five-character box. C names the user harm A only gestures at — the five-character cap applies to the whole string, so once 'FR-' is typed only two characters remain and any region code longer than two characters cannot be entered at all. C also supplies the exact replacement label and hint and the uppercase-plus-hyphen normalisation DR1 applies. A is better on one point C dismisses: A ties the change to the country-list change because DR1's prefix table is keyed on DR1's country labels.

Both: answer Yes to the region-of-origin question, leave the code empty, and the frontend lets you through with no message; DR1 holds you with 'Enter the region of origin code'. Same diff, same message, same one-validator fix. A is more complete on DR1's later gates (hub row and review Continue). C is more honest about its evidence — it records that DR1's origin page was never photographed in its error state and names the observation that would settle the wording. Nothing to choose between them.

Both: the frontend reuses the ports-of-entry list for port of exit; DR1 offers ten animal-approved border control posts. Both band it needs-backend. C is materially more useful — it finds the frontend's own obligation text citing the V4 field spec ('Exit and Entry share the same list') and names the real problem: the V4 spec and Design release 1 disagree, and this ticket is where that gets settled, not a defect to be quietly fixed. A is more precise on the count (78 entries against C's 'about eighty').

Both: DR1 asks purpose, destination country, port of exit and exit date as conditional reveals under the chosen reason; the frontend asks each on its own page behind a second hub task. Both catch that the transit and temporary-admission pairs are asked in the reverse order. C is the fuller ticket — it counts the extra page loads per reason, records that each split-out page says its own name three times (breadcrumb, h1, label), and folds in the hint text those pages carry that DR1's reveals do not. A is better on one consequence C misses: retiring the pages also kills the dead unlinked 'Exit details' hub row.

Both: DR1 heads the page 'Main reason for import' with the question as a visually hidden legend; the frontend promotes the question to the h1. C adds the point A misses — the frontend already calls the page two different things, 'Reason for import' in the breadcrumb and title against the question in the heading, so the fix collapses three places to one name.

Both: four of the eleven internal-market purpose hints drift from DR1 — "it's" for "its", a stray comma, "e.g." for "for example", three missing full stops. Near-identical findings down to the quoted strings and the same one-file fix. A's verification carries one guard rail C does not: the 'traveling' spelling in the Companion animal hint is shared by both sides and must NOT be tidied in the same pass.

Both: choose Internal market, select no purpose, and the frontend advances silently; DR1 stops with 'Select a purpose in the internal market'. C merges this with the identical exit-date gap into one finding (see the inc-083 row). A splits them and is the better ticket for it — two pages, two validators, two copy files. C is better at one thing: it traces the whole enforcement ladder to prove the notification is not actually submittable in this state, so nobody mistakes it for a data-integrity hole.

Both: the exit date can be left blank on a temporary-admission-horses import and the frontend says nothing; DR1 asks with 'Enter an exit date'. C folds it into the purpose finding above rather than giving it an id. A is stronger — it grepped both the frontend and tests repos to prove the string 'Enter an exit date' exists nowhere in the service, and its own verification pulls back the title's overstatement (the journey does stop the user later, just never at the point of the mistake). A also raises the 'Enter a real exit date' / 'Enter a real date' wording here, where C moves it to inc-066.

Both: the destination-country and port-of-exit errors read 'Select the …' where DR1 and GDS style read 'Select a …'. C's version is wider and readier to hand to a developer — it adds the third string on the same theme ('Enter a real exit date' repeating a field name that is already the heading and the label), names all three copy files, and remembers the Welsh files beside them. A instead asks for a service-wide sweep for the same pattern, which is a bigger and vaguer ask.

onlyA.title: The frontend's country list holds only sovereign states; DR1 offers fourteen regions and territories alongside them
onlyA.why: C saw it and ruled it out — this is a judgement split, not a miss. C's verification on inc-072 states plainly that 'the differing country lists are fixture data on both sides', so C treated list contents as non-comparable and scoped its country finding to the control only. A's own verification agrees on the mechanism (the frontend's list is served by the reference-data service with a captured fixture under stub mode) but still raises it, and leaves the sharper question open: dropping Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland may be a DR1 omission rather than a rule. A BA should treat this as one open question, not one confirmed finding — but the user harm A names is real either way, since a trader importing from the Canary Islands, Jersey or French Guiana currently cannot say so.

onlyA.title: The frontend refuses to save the origin page until a country of origin is chosen; DR1 lets the user save what they have
onlyA.why: C missed it. This is the one page in the slice where the frontend is the STRICTER side, and C never asked the question — its inc-075 detail recites 'the origin page's rule set requires a country' as background without ever checking whether DR1 does the same. It does not: DR1 validates only the region code on submit and catches the missing country at the hub and the review page instead. C is capable of finding frontend-stricter differences (it raised the equivalent on transit countries at inc-119), so this is an oversight rather than a policy. A's verification is solid — it read both validators, both hub gates and both review gates.

onlyA.title: The frontend rejects an internal reference containing a space, hyphen or slash; DR1 accepts whatever the user's own system calls the consignment
onlyA.why: C missed it. C's inc-075 detail even mentions in passing that the origin ruleset applies 'two rules to the internal reference' — so C's evidence shows the rules were still there at its capture, it simply never compared them against DR1, which imposes none. No mention of 'underscores' or the 58-character ceiling anywhere in C's backlog. Worth keeping: a trader whose own reference is ACME-2026/01 cannot enter it, and A flags that 58 may be arbitrary and that any surviving limit should be stated in the hint rather than only in an error.

onlyA.title: The frontend explains destination country, port of exit and exit date with guidance DR1 does not have
onlyA.why: Not a miss — it is inside two other C findings without an id of its own. C put the destination-country hint and the leading sentence of the exit-date hint into inc-067 (the reveal move), and the port-of-exit hint into inc-069 (the exit port list), on the reasoning that each hint dies with the change that removes its page. A's separate id is the better ticketing choice if the reveal move is deferred, because the copy fix stands on its own; C's placement is the better sequencing if it is not. Both runs independently spotted that 'Exit and entry share the same port list' becomes untrue once the exit list is narrowed.

matched.note: Certification-purpose hint: both say name the ITAHC instead of "the health certificate". Same diff, same file, same line. A also flags the contraction "You'll" as off-house-style and warns about first use of the abbreviation; C also confirms the sixteen options and their order match. Equally good.

"Change number of animals" link on each species panel. Identical ask. C is better: it enumerates every link in the captured DOM as the falsifier (four links, none reaching consignment details) and explains why it bites — the frontend enforces the count in both directions, so the count-drop refusal tells a trader the number is wrong and gives them nowhere to go. A's extra value is the implementation note that DR1's link carries no return context, so matching DR1 needs nothing more than a bare href.

"Passport number"/"Ear tag number" should read "Passport"/"Ear tag". Both spot that the frontend already uses the short forms in its own saved-animal summary, so a trader is shown one name typing and another reading back. Both leave the worked-example hints as a separate decision. C cites the input ids from the captured DOM; A cites the duplicate label set that unifying would remove. Line-ball.

Identifiers must stop gating submit. Note C filed this under `review`, not `identification` — match on substance, not domain. C is better: it quotes DR1's own stated rule ("Animal identifiers are optional unless multiple species are selected"), names the precise obligation edit (drop `recordCountEquals`), and confirms the animals backend rejects on status not content so no contract change is needed. One flag for the BA: the two runs disagree on the DR1 incomplete-review capture — A lists five error-summary entries (including additional details), C lists exactly four. One of the two mis-read its own screenshot, or the captures were taken at different moments.

No microchip field anywhere in the frontend. C is materially better and correctly banded: it is `needs-backend` because the backend's AnimalIdentifier type codes know only EAR_TAG and PASSPORT, so a microchip entered in the frontend could not reach GBNAG. A bands this `frontend-work` and scopes the change to frontend files only — under-banded, and the plan would stall on landing. A is wider on applicability (horses, cats, dogs and ferrets) where C names only dog and horse; A's scope is the correct one.

Page headings should drop the word "animal" — "Identification details" and "Additional details". Word-for-word the same finding, same two copy files, both defer to the section-caption work landing alongside. C adds that each name feeds h1, breadcrumb and tab title from one string. Nothing to choose between them.

THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL DIFFERENCE IN THIS AREA. Both find that DR1 counts an animal identified only when every identifier for its commodity is filled, where the frontend accepts any one. A states it flatly as `frontend-work` and prescribes changing requires-anyOf to requires-all. C bands it `disputed` and is the only run to spot that the V4 data-fields specification the frontend implements says the opposite in words — the obligation itself carries the line "Field Block - Mandatory to Submit - At least one Animal Identifier" — and that DR1 shows no error, so its behaviour is silent rather than a stated rule. If C is right, A's prescribed change is the wrong change. This needs a ruling from the design authority, and only run C tells the BA that.

Saved animals should read back as a table with a column per identifier, not a run-together summary-list line. Same ask. C is better evidenced: it has a captured DR1 saved state (dr1-animal-identification-details-saved) and cites the partial line-for-line, where A says outright that DR1's populated state was not captured and tells the implementer to read the source instead. C also spots that the row label "Animal 1" repeats as the first row of every commodity line on the page.

Add DR1's "Selected commodities" block above the identification cards. Same ask, same DR1 lines. C is better on the how: it finds that the frontend already builds a Selected commodities table on the consignment-details page and names the view model to reuse, and that the page's one "Add a commodity" link exists but only in the branch that runs when there are no commodities — so it vanishes exactly when it becomes useful. A only notes that the frontend's picker is a checkbox list, not a search, so the Change link's destination differs.

Permanent address should be its own step in the addresses/parties section rather than nine blank fields buried in each animal's identification card. A carries the whole subject in this one finding; C splits it into five (inc-059 to inc-063). Same core conclusion, arrived at independently. C's split is more buildable; A's single finding reads better as a story and is the only one that says DR1's own "are all the animals going to the place of destination?" view is dead code with no callers.

Same-as-place-of-destination as a one-click answer. A folds this into inc-012 as part of the new page; C gives it its own id. Real difference in the prescribed work: C proposes adding the radio inside the existing identification card (a smaller, standalone change), A puts it on the new page it is asking for. A BA should read them together, not pick one.

Guidance copy on the permanent address. A asks for DR1's two-bullet APHA definition and the 48-hour hint. C asks for those and the govukWarningText "Providing a false address is an act of fraud" plus the question heading "Where will their permanent address be?". A missed the fraud warning entirely — the word "fraud" appears nowhere in run A.

"Postal or zip code"/"Telephone number" should read "Postcode or Zip code"/"Phone number" on the permanent-address block. A raises it service-wide across every address form (and explicitly names the permanent-address copy file as one of the two places the strings are authored); C scopes it to this block and additionally catches the missing phone hint "For international numbers include the country code", which A raised only for the private transporter form. Different framings, both right; C catches the hint gap here, A catches the pattern.

onlyA.title: DR1 orders each commodity's identifier boxes by that commodity's own list; the frontend uses one fixed order for every animal
onlyA.why: C missed it, and had the evidence in hand. C's verification note on inc-056 records the frontend's three cattle fields as "Passport number", "Tattoo", "Ear tag number" and DR1's two as "Ear tag", "Passport" — it read both orders off the screenshots and never authored the ordering difference. No C finding mentions identifier order. A's point is load-bearing: a global order has nowhere to put a microchip that DR1 asks for first on some commodities and not at all on others, so this has to be settled before the microchip work.

onlyA.title: DR1 asks nothing about identifying a commodity with no identifier type; the frontend falls back to free-text identification details and an animal description
onlyA.why: C missed the substance. Run C never mentions fish on the identification page at all — "Fish (0301)" appears only in its commodity-picker finding. The half of A's finding about making the identification task row conditional does have a C id (inc-044, hub domain, well argued and arguably better on the mechanics of dropping the row), but the free-text fallback fields — the two boxes asking a trader to describe one salmon in prose — have no C counterpart.

onlyA.title: The identification page's green button reads 'Save and finish' where DR1 and every other page read 'Save and continue'
onlyA.why: C missed it. The string "Save and finish" appears nowhere in run C's backlog. Small on its own, but A explains why it is not free-standing: it collides with the in-card button wording in inc-075, and doing that one without this one leaves two identically labelled buttons on the page doing different things.

onlyA.title: 'Save and add another' shows on every record including a consignment of one; DR1 hides it for one animal and says 'Save and finish' on the last
onlyA.why: C missed it. C mentions "Save and add another" only as a landmark when locating the permanent-address block inside the card, never as a difference. A's evidence is three captured states — one-of-one, last-of-two, and at-maximum — showing the words never tell the trader what pressing them will do.

onlyA.title: The frontend asks for a tattoo on every cow; DR1 asks a cow only for an ear tag and a passport
onlyA.why: C missed it, and this is the most surprising miss in the area, because C's own verification note for inc-056 states that the frontend labels three cattle fields and DR1 labels two. C compared the labels of the fields both sides have and never asked why the frontend has an extra one. The fix is one name off one allowlist.

onlyA.title: The frontend asks the unweaned-animals question of horses; DR1 asks it only of cattle and pigs
onlyA.why: C missed it and asserted the opposite. C's inc-053 says the page carries "the same unweaned-animals question with the same hint", and its verification note says "the unweaned question and its hint match word for word". C compared the copy and never compared which commodities make the question appear. A BA reading only run C would conclude this question is at parity; it is not — a horses-only consignment is asked a question DR1 does not ask, and cannot continue without answering it.

onlyC.title: The frontend refuses a lowered animal count while identification records exist; DR1 accepts it and shows only that many records
onlyC.why: A missed it, having seen the rule. A's inc-023 (blank animal counts) mentions the count-drop check in passing as a knock-on, so run A knew the validator existed and never compared it to DR1 or raised it. C has a dedicated capture for it (fe-consignment-details-count-drop-error) and establishes DR1 runs four validators on that page, none of which reads saved identifiers. This is a genuine dead end for a trader who miscounts, and it pairs with the Change-number-of-animals link both runs found.

onlyC.title: Both questions on the additional details page are set one size smaller than DR1, so they do not read as questions
onlyC.why: A missed it, and it is the kind of finding A was otherwise good at — A authored exactly this comparison for the origin page (small labels and legends against DR1's medium plus app-eu-heading-m). It simply did not run the same check on this page. Two classes in one template; sixteen certification radios and two unweaned radios currently run together as one list.

onlyC.title: The frontend asks which country the animals will permanently live in; DR1 asks for eight permanent-address fields and no country
onlyC.why: A missed it. A's inc-012 lists "country" among the frontend's blank inputs but never notices DR1's new-address reveal has eight inputs and no select at all.
